name: CAP Theorem
intent: When a network failure splits a distributed system, it must choose between answering every request (availability) and never returning wrong or conflicting data (consistency).
scenario: Two database nodes in different data centres each hold a copy of the same value. Clients can reach either one. Then the link between the data centres goes down.
problem: Copies of data on several machines must talk to each other to stay identical. Networks do fail, so at some point the nodes cannot talk. A client then asks one of them for data, or tries to change it. The node cannot know what the other side is doing, and has to decide what to do anyway.

howItWorks.title: The three properties
howItWorks.text: Consistency means every read sees the most recent write (as if there were one copy). Availability means every request to a working node gets a non-error answer. Partition tolerance means the system keeps working even when messages between nodes are lost.

howItWorks.title: Partitions are not optional
howItWorks.text: On a real network, partitions happen: cables fail, switches misbehave, data centres lose contact. So a distributed system must tolerate them. The real choice is not 'pick two of three' but what to give up when a partition occurs.

howItWorks.title: CP: stay consistent, give up availability
howItWorks.text: During a partition the node refuses to answer (or to accept writes) if it cannot confirm that its data is current. Clients get errors, but nobody ever sees stale or conflicting data. Examples: systems that need a majority quorum, or those storing money.

howItWorks.title: AP: stay available, give up consistency
howItWorks.text: Each node keeps answering with what it has and accepts writes locally. Both sides stay up, but they can drift apart. When the partition heals the system must reconcile, for example by last-write-wins, which can drop a write. Examples: shopping carts, social feeds, DNS.

howItWorks.title: Without a partition you can have both, but there is still a trade-off
howItWorks.text: When the network is healthy, systems usually offer both. Even then there is a trade-off between latency and consistency: waiting for other nodes to confirm makes every operation slower (this is the extension known as PACELC).

pros: Gives a precise way to reason about what a distributed store can promise
Forces an explicit, per-feature decision about failure behaviour
Explains why different databases behave so differently under failure
Choices can be mixed: strict for payments, relaxed for likes
cons: Often over-simplified to 'pick any two', which is misleading
Says nothing about performance or about normal operation
Real systems sit on a spectrum, not at pure CP or pure AP
AP designs push conflict resolution onto the application
whenToUse: Choose CP for money, inventory counts, locks and anything where a wrong answer is worse than no answer
Choose AP for carts, feeds, presence, caches and metrics where being up matters more than being exact
Use the framing early, when deciding how a data store should behave on failure
whenNotToUse: On a single-node database: there is no partition between copies to reason about
As the only tool: it does not cover latency, durability or transactions
To justify vague claims like 'our system is CA': with real networks that is not a choice
pitfalls: Believing a system can give up partition tolerance and be 'CA' on a network that can fail
Treating CP or AP as a property of a whole product, when it is often tunable per operation
Last-write-wins silently discarding a customer's update
Assuming 'available' means 'fast' or 'correct': it only means 'answers'
